title: Solid 2.0 Effects + Async Tour
intent: Explain why Solid 2.0 split effects into compute/apply phases and how async readiness flows through effects, scheduling, and boundaries.

steps.title: Concept: compute before apply
steps.body:
# Solid 2.0: Split Effects

The old single callback mixed two jobs:

- read reactive sources and discover dependencies
- mutate the outside world

Solid 2.0 separates them:

```ts
createEffect(
  () => source(),
  value => doSideEffect(value)
)
```

This lets the runtime discover all dependencies and pending async before any user side effect runs.

steps.title: RFC rationale
steps.body: The RFC frames split effects as part of a broader reactivity model: stricter writes, read warnings, batching, async, and boundaries.

anchors.note: The RFC states the full motivation: stricter writes, top-level read warnings, microtask batching, and split effects for async and boundaries.
This is the API-level reason: compute records dependencies; effect runs after all compute phases in the batch.
The single-callback default was explicitly rejected for async and boundary semantics.

steps.title: Effect types and public wrapper
steps.body: The public API exposes the split directly: compute returns a value, apply consumes it later.

anchors.note: ComputeFunction and EffectFunction encode the split: compute returns the value; effect consumes it and may return cleanup.
The docs on the public createEffect API tell users where reactive reads and imperative writes belong.
createEffect rejects the old single-argument form in dev and forwards compute/apply/error into the core effect primitive.
createRenderEffect uses the same split primitive but without user scheduling; it is for renderer-level synchronous work.
createTrackedEffect preserves the single-callback shape only as an explicit advanced escape hatch.

steps.title: effect() creates a lazy computed
steps.body: Internally, an effect is represented as a computed node plus owner/effect-specific fields.

anchors.note: An Effect is both a Computed node and an Owner, with storage for apply callback, cleanup, previous value, and queue type.
effect() wraps the compute half in computed(..., { lazy: true }). Its equals hook marks the node modified and enqueues runEffect.
The apply/error callbacks and effect queue type are stored on the computed node.
Creation recomputes the compute phase immediately, then schedules or runs the apply phase unless defer is set.
runEffect is the apply half: cleanup old side effect, run _effectFn(value, prev), store returned cleanup, then commit prevValue.

steps.title: Status handling from effect nodes
steps.body: Effect nodes participate in async/error propagation instead of treating pending async as an ordinary value.

anchors.note: Effect nodes customize _notifyStatus so async pending/errors are either surfaced to user error handlers or propagated to boundary queues.

steps.title: recompute() runs tracked compute
steps.body: The compute phase runs under tracking context, captures dependencies, and converts pending async into status propagation.

anchors.note: recompute sets context to the computed node and enables tracking before invoking the compute function.
The compute function runs here. Its result is routed through handleAsync unless the computation registered async internally.
NotReadyError marks the node pending and propagates status instead of treating pending async as a normal value.
After successful compute, dependencies are reconciled and changed values notify subscribers via insertSubs.

steps.title: Effect creation next to recompute
steps.body: This cross-file step connects the effect primitive to the generic recomputation machinery.

anchors.note: effect() builds a computed node around the compute half.
recompute invokes that compute half and hands its result to handleAsync.

steps.title: handleAsync detects pending work
steps.body: Async values produced during compute are converted into suspension and later resumption.

anchors.note: handleAsync accepts the compute result and detects Promise-like values or AsyncIterables. Synchronous values pass through.
For unresolved Promises, Solid initializes a transition and throws NotReadyError from the compute path.
AsyncIterables follow the same model: if no synchronous value is available, throw NotReadyError and resume later.

steps.title: Async resolution writes back
steps.body: Once async work resolves, Solid writes the result back into the graph and resumes blocked dependents.

anchors.note: asyncWrite is the resume path. It ignores stale async results, commits the resolved value, settles pending sources, schedules and flushes.
settlePendingSource walks dependents that were blocked by this async source and reschedules them.
notifyStatus propagates pending/error state through dependents and boundary queues.

steps.title: Microtask scheduling
steps.body: Scheduling batches graph work so reads and effects observe the post-batch state.

anchors.note: schedule() batches work onto a microtask unless a flush is already running.
flush() explicitly drains scheduled work and active transitions. This is why reads update after the batch, not immediately after setters.

steps.title: Flush ordering
steps.body: The scheduler preserves the invariant that compute/finalization happens before render/user effects run.

anchors.note: GlobalQueue.flush runs pure recomputation first, finalizes pending nodes, then runs render effects and user effects.
Lane effects only run when their lane has no pending async. This is where async prevents premature apply callbacks.
commitPendingNodes moves pending values into committed values and marks effect nodes modified before apply queues run.

steps.title: Boundary queue basics
steps.body: Boundaries contain pending/error status by running subtrees under specialized queues.

anchors.note: boundaryComputed creates computed nodes with custom status propagation masks.
createBoundChildren runs a subtree under a child queue so pending/error status can be contained by a boundary.
CollectionQueue is the boundary queue type used to collect pending sources and coordinate reveal/loading state.

steps.title: Public Loading component
steps.body: The public component API exposes async pending as a structural boundary concept.

anchors.note: <Loading> is a thin component wrapper over createLoadingBoundary. Async pending is structural, not a resource.loading flag.

steps.title: Hydration-aware createLoadingBoundary
steps.body: Hydration can resume or force fallback state before normal boundary behavior takes over.

anchors.note: On the client, createLoadingBoundary delegates to the core boundary unless hydration-specific serialized state must be resumed.
During hydration, serialized boundary state can force fallback until streamed or asset-backed async work resumes.

steps.title: Call path summary
steps.body:
# End-To-End Path

1. User calls `createEffect(compute, apply)`.
2. `signals.ts` forwards both functions to `effect()`.
3. `effect.ts` creates a lazy `computed` node for the compute phase.
4. `recompute()` sets tracking context and runs `compute(prev)`.
5. If compute returns a Promise or AsyncIterable, `handleAsync()` throws `NotReadyError` while registering pending work.
6. `notifyStatus()` propagates pending to dependents and boundaries.
7. `Loading`/boundary queues hold apply work while pending async exists.
8. When async resolves, `asyncWrite()` commits/reschedules and flushes.
9. Scheduler finalizes computed values, then runs `runEffect()`.
10. `runEffect()` executes `apply(value, prev)` untracked and stores cleanup.

The important invariant: side effects run after the graph has established dependencies and async readiness.

steps.title: Main implementation files together
steps.body: The core implementation path crosses effect construction, async detection/suspension, and eventual application of the side effect.

anchors.note: Create effect node.
Apply side effect.
Detect async.
Suspend with NotReadyError.
